reflections.lifeSketch: A 58-year-old married apartment caretaker who enjoyed repairing radios.
reflections.teaser: I kept promising myself a quieter year.
reflections.reflection: I kept promising myself a quieter year. You would ask me to sit beside you, and I would say, “In a minute.” I wish I had sat down.

reflections.lifeSketch: A 46-year-old parent and night student living in a small inland town.
reflections.teaser: My application was still in the drawer.
reflections.reflection: My application was still in the drawer. I had good reasons to wait, and some frightened ones. I wish I had told someone which were which, instead of pretending I had stopped wanting to learn.

reflections.lifeSketch: A 72-year-old retired laboratory technician who joined a neighborhood choir at sixty.
reflections.teaser: I went to the rehearsal on Tuesday.
reflections.reflection: I went to the rehearsal on Tuesday. My voice shook through every song, and I returned the next week anyway. Those ordinary evenings became a whole part of my life that I nearly never met.

reflections.lifeSketch: A 39-year-old graphic designer living far from an old friend.
reflections.teaser: I knew her number without looking.
reflections.reflection: I knew her number without looking. Somehow that made calling feel less urgent, as if knowing where someone was meant we were still close. I kept the number longer than I kept the friendship.

reflections.lifeSketch: A 64-year-old low-income tenant who tended a shared courtyard and worked irregular shifts.
reflections.teaser: The trip never became affordable.
reflections.reflection: The trip never became affordable. I do not blame myself for that. But there were afternoons in the courtyard I spent ashamed of staying, while my neighbors were making room for me at their table.

reflections.lifeSketch: A 51-year-old wheelchair user, translator, and amateur percussionist living with a partner.
reflections.teaser: We stopped waiting for the perfect room.
reflections.reflection: We stopped waiting for the perfect room. We moved the chairs and invited everyone over. The music was uneven, the neighbors complained once, and I am glad we made a place for it.

reflections.lifeSketch: A 79-year-old married woman who ran a small stationery shop with her wife.
reflections.teaser: We had supper together for forty years.
reflections.reflection: We had supper together for forty years. When I think about my life now, I keep hearing her put two plates on the table.

reflections.lifeSketch: A 61-year-old regional manager and father of an adult son.
reflections.teaser: I answered every question except the quiet ones.
reflections.reflection: I answered every question except the quiet ones. My son would stay in the doorway after asking for the car keys. I wish I had noticed that he was sometimes waiting for an invitation to stay.

reflections.lifeSketch: A 43-year-old baker sharing a home with two longtime friends.
reflections.teaser: We argued about the dishes until the last week.
reflections.reflection: We argued about the dishes until the last week. I hope they remember the other things too: the spare keys, the soup, how none of us had to explain a bad day before sitting down.

reflections.lifeSketch: An 83-year-old widower who met a neighbor every morning for a walk.
reflections.teaser: He always slowed down at my gate.
reflections.reflection: He always slowed down at my gate. We talked about very little, which is how we eventually talked about everything. I had not expected another friendship to become so important after seventy.

reflections.lifeSketch: A 56-year-old ceramics teacher estranged from a former close friend.
reflections.teaser: I wanted her to call first.
reflections.reflection: I wanted her to call first. Years passed while I rehearsed how gracious I would be when she finally apologized. There were things I needed to say too, and I never made room for them.

reflections.lifeSketch: A 34-year-old sound technician who moved cities often and regularly visited a younger sister.
reflections.teaser: My sister knew which train I took.
reflections.reflection: My sister knew which train I took. I wish I had stayed longer on those visits. Still, we made something of the hours we had, and I do not want my wanting more to erase them.

reflections.lifeSketch: A 67-year-old accountant who kept careful household budgets and loved restoring furniture.
reflections.teaser: I kept waiting until I had more to give.
reflections.reflection: I kept waiting until I had more to give. There is money left. What hurts is remembering who needed help while I kept moving the amount that would finally make me feel secure.

reflections.lifeSketch: A 45-year-old school receptionist who hosted a weekly shared lunch.
reflections.teaser: I always made an extra portion.
reflections.reflection: I always made an extra portion. Sometimes nobody came, and I ate it the next day. Sometimes a person sat down who had not spoken to anyone all morning, and we had lunch.

reflections.lifeSketch: A 70-year-old retired lawyer and grandparent who volunteered at a reading group.
reflections.teaser: I liked being thanked more than I admitted.
reflections.reflection: I liked being thanked more than I admitted. Once I began noticing that, I tried listening before offering help. Some people needed things I could not provide, and some needed me to stop deciding for them.

reflections.lifeSketch: A 48-year-old gardener who shared a home with a cousin.
reflections.teaser: I gave advice when he asked for company.
reflections.reflection: I gave advice when he asked for company. It made me feel useful and let me leave quickly. I wish I had stayed through the awkward silence long enough to hear what he was trying to tell me.

reflections.lifeSketch: A 62-year-old bus dispatcher who ran a small informal tool lending shelf.
reflections.teaser: The drill came back with a different handle.
reflections.reflection: The drill came back with a different handle. I laughed because it worked better. I liked seeing what people could make with something I owned, and eventually I stopped thinking of it as only mine.

reflections.lifeSketch: A 37-year-old university librarian learning to set boundaries with an extended family.
reflections.teaser: I finally learned to leave some evenings empty.
reflections.reflection: I finally learned to leave some evenings empty. Saying yes to everyone had made me resent the people I loved. The help I could offer honestly was smaller, but I was there for it.

reflections.lifeSketch: A 59-year-old community swimming instructor and foster parent.
reflections.teaser: There were mornings when I hated getting up.
reflections.reflection: There were mornings when I hated getting up. Then someone would be relieved to see me. That mattered more than I knew.

reflections.lifeSketch: A 76-year-old retired archivist cataloguing local photographs with younger volunteers.
reflections.teaser: There are still boxes without labels.
reflections.reflection: There are still boxes without labels. For years I imagined finishing would make me calm. Now I think of the people who learned beside me, and I am less afraid of leaving the last boxes to them.

reflections.lifeSketch: A 54-year-old successful restaurant owner who once enjoyed sketching strangers.
reflections.teaser: I turned everything I enjoyed into a target.
reflections.reflection: I turned everything I enjoyed into a target. Even drawing on a Sunday became something I had to get better at. I miss the person who could fill a page and throw it away without feeling behind.

reflections.lifeSketch: A 41-year-old warehouse coordinator in long-term alcohol recovery who maintained friendships outside work.
reflections.teaser: I became someone my friends could rely on.
reflections.reflection: I became someone my friends could rely on. It happened through small arrangements: arriving when I said I would, returning a call, telling the truth when I could not manage. I am proud of that life.

reflections.lifeSketch: A 65-year-old musician and parent who changed careers twice.
reflections.teaser: I never found one thing to be.
reflections.reflection: I never found one thing to be. I taught, repaired instruments, raised a child, and started over. Some changes were forced on me. Even so, there were moments in each life when I felt useful and awake.

reflections.lifeSketch: A 47-year-old civil engineer who mentored apprentices and hid uncertainty from colleagues.
reflections.teaser: I was good at looking certain.
reflections.reflection: I was good at looking certain. People trusted me, and I began treating every doubt as something shameful. I wish I had asked more questions while there were still people beside me who could answer.

reflections.lifeSketch: A 60-year-old clothing shop owner with a close circle of longtime neighbors.
reflections.teaser: I kept measuring our house against other houses.
reflections.reflection: I kept measuring our house against other houses. Meanwhile, people I loved were laughing in the kitchen. I was there with them, but part of me was always inspecting a life I did not have.

reflections.lifeSketch: A 73-year-old former executive who loved learning traditional dances with friends.
reflections.teaser: I was the least graceful person in the class.
reflections.reflection: I was the least graceful person in the class. Nobody needed me to be impressive there. I learned their names, lost the rhythm, tried again, and found a kind of ease I had missed for years.

reflections.lifeSketch: A 38-year-old freelance illustrator renting a room and rebuilding savings.
reflections.teaser: I wanted a room of my own.
reflections.reflection: I wanted a room of my own. That was a reasonable thing to want. I wish I had not turned every photograph of someone else’s home into evidence that I had failed at being alive.

reflections.lifeSketch: A 68-year-old retired teacher with a younger brother.
reflections.teaser: My brother never knew we were competing.
reflections.reflection: My brother never knew we were competing. He would tell me good news and I would spend the evening feeling smaller. I lost so many chances to be happy with him over a contest I invented.

reflections.lifeSketch: A 52-year-old wheelchair user and local history researcher who hosted friends for games.
reflections.teaser: Our games took most of Sunday.
reflections.reflection: Our games took most of Sunday. Some weeks I arrived still bitter about an argument or a rejection. I loved being expected there anyway, with my terrible strategies and extra snacks, without having to become cheerful before I could belong.

reflections.lifeSketch: A 44-year-old photographer who lived with a partner and cared for an aging aunt.
reflections.teaser: I still wanted people to like my work.
reflections.reflection: I still wanted people to like my work. I do not think that was wrong. But the afternoon my aunt fell asleep holding my hand mattered to me without anyone else ever seeing it.

reflections.lifeSketch: An 81-year-old former postal worker who cultivated herbs on a balcony.
reflections.teaser: The mint survived every winter.
reflections.reflection: The mint survived every winter. I would crush a leaf between my fingers before making tea. There were larger events in my life, of course, but that small familiar smell keeps returning to me now.

reflections.lifeSketch: A 49-year-old cleaner living on a tight income with an adult niece.
reflections.teaser: We listened to the rain through a leaking roof.
reflections.reflection: We listened to the rain through a leaking roof. I wanted the landlord to fix it, and I am still angry that he never did. I also remember my niece’s laugh when we ran out of bowls.

reflections.lifeSketch: A 63-year-old amateur runner and parent who often tracked personal achievements.
reflections.teaser: I hardly remember the routes without a stopwatch.
reflections.reflection: I hardly remember the routes without a stopwatch. There were trees changing color and friends talking beside me. I wish I had let a few mornings count for nothing except being outside together.

reflections.lifeSketch: A 57-year-old seamstress living with a close friend and two cats.
reflections.teaser: We opened the window while we worked.
reflections.reflection: We opened the window while we worked. The street would send us arguments, music, the bread delivery. It was an ordinary room and an ordinary life, and I liked the way I belonged inside it.

reflections.lifeSketch: A 36-year-old graduate student and parent who enjoyed swimming and neighborhood markets.
reflections.teaser: My child loved the cracked blue bowl.
reflections.reflection: My child loved the cracked blue bowl. I kept meaning to replace it. Now I remember how seriously he carried it to breakfast, and how a household can become yours through things nobody would choose from a shop.

reflections.lifeSketch: A 74-year-old former freight coordinator who learned to bake with a neighbor.
reflections.teaser: The first loaf was almost inedible.
reflections.reflection: The first loaf was almost inedible. We ate the middle and made another the following week. I am glad I kept learning things that would never appear on a certificate or earn me anything.

reflections.lifeSketch: A 66-year-old divorced parent who rebuilt contact with an adult daughter.
reflections.teaser: She agreed to meet me for coffee.
reflections.reflection: She agreed to meet me for coffee. We did not repair twenty years that afternoon. I listened, badly at first, then better. I am grateful for that beginning even though I wanted more than she could give.

reflections.lifeSketch: A 53-year-old delivery coordinator and oldest of three siblings.
reflections.teaser: I could explain every hurtful thing I said.
reflections.reflection: I could explain every hurtful thing I said. I thought an explanation should make the hurt disappear. I wish I had spent less time defending my reasons and more time hearing what living with them had cost.

reflections.lifeSketch: A 78-year-old retired cook who renewed a friendship after a long disagreement.
reflections.teaser: We started again with a bag of oranges.
reflections.reflection: We started again with a bag of oranges. Neither of us made a speech. Later we did talk about what happened, and it hurt, but by then we remembered why we had wanted each other in our lives.

reflections.lifeSketch: A 42-year-old groundskeeper in recovery from alcohol dependence who stayed close to a sponsor and sibling.
reflections.teaser: Some people never answered my letters.
reflections.reflection: Some people never answered my letters. They had their reasons, and recovery did not entitle me to a reply. I kept changing what I could, with help, and learned to live without calling that change a bargain.

reflections.lifeSketch: A 71-year-old retired publisher whose closest friendship ended over a business disagreement.
reflections.teaser: I told the story until I was blameless.
reflections.reflection: I told the story until I was blameless. Each time I left out another detail that made me uncomfortable. By the end, I had almost forgotten the apology I owed, though I had never stopped missing him.

reflections.lifeSketch: A 55-year-old counselor who kept firm distance from a harmful former partner and built a new household.
reflections.teaser: I stopped waiting for the apology to arrive.
reflections.reflection: I stopped waiting for the apology to arrive. I kept the distance I needed and made a home with other people. Peace came slowly, and it did not require pretending that what happened had been all right.

reflections.lifeSketch: A 69-year-old retired boat builder living with a spouse and close to several grandchildren.
reflections.teaser: I was happy.
reflections.reflection: I was happy. I still wanted more time. There are people I hadn’t finished loving, and small plans I was looking forward to keeping with them.

reflections.lifeSketch: An 86-year-old retired mathematics teacher who lived alone and welcomed regular visits from friends.
reflections.teaser: I do not need another grand chapter.
reflections.reflection: I do not need another grand chapter. I have loved people, made mistakes, learned their names again after losing touch. I would enjoy another morning, but I can look at the mornings I had without turning away.

reflections.lifeSketch: A 33-year-old landscape architect living with friends and engaged to a longtime partner.
reflections.teaser: I am still angry about leaving.
reflections.reflection: I am still angry about leaving. There are good things I can remember, and people who have been gentle with me. Neither makes this feel fair. I am trying to let gratitude and anger sit together.

reflections.lifeSketch: A 75-year-old former rail administrator who kept journals and cared for a garden.
reflections.teaser: There are pages I wish I could rewrite.
reflections.reflection: There are pages I wish I could rewrite. I cannot make those choices kinder now. I have told the truth about some of them, and I am still learning to stay with what the truth leaves unfinished.

reflections.lifeSketch: A 64-year-old potter who taught informally and enjoyed long conversations with friends.
reflections.teaser: Someone else can finish the glaze tests.
reflections.reflection: Someone else can finish the glaze tests. I left the notes where they can find them. I enjoyed the questions more than the answers, and I like imagining the workshop noisy again when I am gone.

reflections.lifeSketch: A 58-year-old hospital interpreter who lived with a partner and loved evening walks.
reflections.teaser: I do not know how to say goodbye well.
reflections.reflection: I do not know how to say goodbye well. Sometimes I ask about the weather because I want an ordinary conversation. If that is what you remember, please know I was glad you were in the room.
